rv.q: It’s a very clever play, buoyed by lively performances and a director willing to take risks.
Lynn Nottage's latest play is a tender meditation on second chances and the power of food to heal, anchored by a powerhouse performance from Uzo Aduba.
Lynn Nottage's latest play is a warm-hearted meditation on second chances and the sustaining power of food, elevated by superb performances from Uzo Aduba and an exceptional ensemble.
What Lynn Nottage has accomplished in 'Clyde's' is the creation of a workplace dramedy that manages to be both earthily funny and spiritually nourishing.
The stage is her sandwich, and she slathers it with relish.
Though it’s still about dark things, including prison, drugs, homelessness and poverty, it somehow turns them into bright comedy.
Lynn Nottage improbably turns the lunchtime staple into the storytelling engine of 'Clyde's,' her deceptively simple flavor-bomb of a new comedy.
The camaraderie among the kitchen workers gives the play a jovial warmth, and the performances are impeccable.

Ms. Nottage has created a vivid world populated by richly drawn characters, each carrying burdens of past mistakes and present struggles, yet all finding moments of grace in the simple act of cooking together.
The play is well-acted and has moments of genuine warmth, but it's also repetitive and overstuffed with characters who don't get enough individual attention.
Her play shows you characters who transcend, but it all seems far off, at a comically delineated distance.
Lynn Nottage's latest play is a testament to the power of second chances, anchored by brilliant performances that find hope in the most unlikely places.
Directed by Kate Whoriskey, the author's go-to collaborator, the production cooks on all burners.
The rich economy of the writing is the real joy in Clyde’s.
Everyone else is—to borrow a word from Nottage's kitchen—sublime.
The chief delight of this production is the art and craft of the theater making, by an extraordinarily talented cast.
Dialog is Nottage's strong suit here, and the pitch-perfect cast members, under Kate Whoriskey's solid direction, play it to the hilt.
A combination of witty dialogue, outsize characters, and zany staging creates a madcap world that keeps us laughing while addressing real-world problems with seriousness and sophistication.

But at its best, “Clyde’s” is a relatable, rambunctious, feel-good work that optimistically preaches a path to self-redemption.
Perhaps that’s why Clyde, played to a deliciously evil fare-thee-well by Aduba, is pitched at such an outlandish extreme: She’s the cayenne that keeps this recipe from overdosing on sugar.

If this engaging production leaves out a few garnishes, it still serves up a finger-licking good time with a few stirring insights on the side.
Clyde’s is quite simply, that tantalizingly piquant.
As the dangerous and intimidating Clyde, she gives an indelible performance; just try to take your eyes off of her when she is onstage.
A bold gamble that pays off handsomely in trash talk, crackling tension, and scathing hilarity.
Aduba is a delightfully horrible boss, but Clyde’s would be a more satisfying meal if we had a more fully-realized Clyde.
By the story's conclusion we are nearly as worn down as the workers from this relentless battle between cruelty and hope.
